title: Research deep enough to bet on
description: Use Strawberry to investigate questions, map markets, build structured evidence, and turn current sources into useful research.
introduction: Research rarely stays in one place. The useful source might be a company site, a report, a database, or an internal doc from three years ago. The hard part is keeping the question, the sources, and the argument connected as it grows.

Strawberry can search the web, work through sites you already have access to, and compare what it finds against your own files. Instead of a pile of links, you get a sourced shortlist, a market map, a briefing, or an updated spreadsheet.

blocks.text: Not sure where to begin? Your companion can look at the question, sources, or unfinished research in front of you and suggest a useful skill to try first.

skill.context: Use the research and sources already in front of me to choose a useful first workflow.

blocks.text: Start with something you genuinely need to know: why a category is changing, whether a competitor's claim holds up, which companies fit a thesis, or what an unfamiliar topic means for a decision. Strawberry can do the investigation across current sources and return a concise view of what seems true, what is contested, why it matters, and what still needs evidence.

rows: A concise cited brief with the strongest answer, implications, and open questions
A clear comparison of what is supported, disputed, stale, or still missing
A decision with too much material around it
The few findings that should change the decision, with links back to the evidence

blocks.text: When the question centers on one company, Strawberry can build a current, source-linked brief around what you actually need to understand rather than filling a generic profile.

items.context: Research this company around the question or decision I need help with.

blocks.text: The useful result may be a brief, comparison, evidence-backed recommendation, or a clear conclusion that the available research does not support a confident answer. If a map or dataset would make the evidence easier to use, the same work can continue into those formats without beginning again.

A market map is more than a list of companies. It should explain which categories matter, how the important entities relate, what the current research covers, and what the landscape means for the decision in front of you. Strawberry can test a proposed taxonomy on a varied first set, then expand the accepted definition across current sources.

items.title: Map the broader landscape
items.text: Build a sourced view of the categories, entities, relationships, signals, coverage, uncertainty, and implications shaping a market.

skill.context: Map this market as a sourced landscape built around the decision I need to make.

items.title: Map a startup ecosystem
items.text: Focus the map on startups, investors, associations, experts, and the relationships around an investment question.

skill.context: Map the startups, investors, experts, and relationships shaping this ecosystem.

blocks.text: When the same fields appear across many pages, a dataset is more useful than another summary. Strawberry can move through directories, search results, product pages, public records, PDFs, and approved signed-in tools, validate a representative first set, and then complete the full scope without hiding missing values or failed matches.

items.context: Agree the schema, validate a varied first set, and turn the full web source into a clean dataset.

blocks.text: The result keeps source links beside the rows, makes coverage and gaps explicit, and can continue into a spreadsheet or approved connected destination after review.

The final artifact should make the evidence easier to understand, not merely move it into a prettier file. Strawberry can turn the reviewed work into a cited brief, comparison, spreadsheet, or recommendation while keeping the sources and open questions close.

When the audience needs a presentation, the research and deck remain separate jobs. First settle the evidence and argument; then turn them into a visual story without reopening the investigation or losing the source trail.

items.context: Turn these reviewed findings into a polished, evidence-grounded presentation.

blocks.text: Once the team trusts the source set, definitions, taxonomy, schema, and review points, save the method instead of rebuilding it from the final artifact. A Routine can check for meaningful changes on a useful cadence and stop when a source, scope, access condition, or definition no longer matches the accepted setup.

items.context: Turn a trusted research method into a shared team workflow with clear sources, ownership, review points, and stop conditions.
